message:
This past weekend's storm provided some good riding conditions near and above treeline. The current high pressure weather coupled with soft riding conditions have made for some great days in the backcountry. But don't get lulled into complacency. We still have a Persistent Slab avalanche problem near and above treeline. There have been 98 reported avalanches in the past week. 37 of these were human-triggered. The most suspect slopes are where previous wind-drifting has occurred. These slopes are predominantly at higher elevations and on leeward aspects, where stiffer slabs are hidden beneath the softer snow surface. Of note, many of these avalanches have been triggered remotely or sympathetically. This is in-line with Persistent Slab avalanche characteristics. Subsequently, it behooves you to give a wide birth to steep slopes the have seen previous wind-loading (west through north to east facing, near and above treeline). Also avoid travelling underneath these slopes, even if you are on more mellow terrain.

Below treeline the winter snowpack is supportive and provides good riding and safer travel conditions. But LOW danger isn't NO danger. This small slab avalanche was trigger yesterday buy a snowmobiler below treeline in the Southern San Juans: https://avalanche.state.co.us/reports/observation/b299c7b2-6ebd-4c5c-97e7-6577128b8f55

Images.caption: Following strong winds and modest snowfall on November 17th, we saw our first rash of human-triggered Persistent Slab avalanches. Some were remotely-triggered and one even temporarily caught a skier. Saturday, November 22nd, brought another wave of human-triggered avalanches following a modest load of new snowfall. Our persistent slab avalanche problem is here to stay for the time being and will require patience to manage.

Look closely and you'll see a crown on the shady shoulder of Treasure Mountain. This avalanche was remote-triggered and indicates that we now have a connected slab in the near treeline band that is capable of propagating a collapse across a distance.

Our most impressive avalanche from Saturday comes from the South Fork of Cement Creek, where a skier-triggered a small avalanche on the distant shoulder in this image, and then it propagated over 700 feet across the slope, with a crown that wrapped around the bowl just below the ridgeline. The avalanche failed in just the new snow, where it rested on weak snow, but it flushed all the way to the valley bottom. This is a dangerous avalanche and a sign that things have changed in our mountains.

message:
Following our all-too-familiar Persistent Slab avalanche script, a loading event last weekend on our now-buried early November weak layer produced a quick spike in avalanches, followed by slow drawn out down trend in activity.

This past week 70 avalanches were reported, with 44 of those on Saturday. By Tuesday the daily count was down to 5, and none so far on Wednesday.

Given that usual script, we're probably not done with this avalanche cycle. The next phase often involves people growing comfortable with the conditions, stepping out into as-yet untouched terrain, and popping out a "surprise" avalanche.

To avoid a surprise, keep your terrain use focused where the snowpack lacks a wind-drifted stiff layer below last weekend's fluffy snow. The November 17th southerly wind was the primary slab-building event, so the most problematic features are those that picked up a drift that day. As a generalization, avoid steep northerly and easterly slopes below ridgelines, and seek out wind-sheltered areas, which will also hold the softest snow surfaces

message:
Happy Thanksgiving from everyone at the Colorado Avalanche Information Center. Even though it has been a dry fall, I am very thankful for the calm, sunny days and blue skies we have experienced in November. Hiking for fieldwork has been very pleasant, enjoying a slower pace of life and some fun wildlife sightings that I may have whizzed past if I were on skis.  However, I am also thankful that a change in weather pattern is coming. Saturday should see the first major snowfall for some areas of the Northern Mountains. Areas that perform well on northwest flow, like the Flat Top Mountains, Park Range, Cameron Pass, and Northern Front Range, could accumulate a foot of snow. A stormy outlook continues through next week.

Until then, the only areas where you could get into trouble are small areas of firmer snow where winds have created rounded drifts. These are very isolated and close to ridgelines at elevations above about 12,000 feet. Unfortunately, these places are tempting to ride or are at the top of gullies or ice climbs. They should be easy to identify and work around.  

Small incremental storms over the last week and stronger winds before the weekend mean we have a nice layer of white on most northwest-, north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes. If you set foot on these slopes, you will see the blanket is pretty thin. In most places, it is less than 15cm thick and generally made up of facets of varying sizes. Facets are the weak grains that form the base of our snowpack in most seasons. They're not an issue right now, but once a slab forms, they will be a nasty, widespread weak layer. The slab is hopefully on its way with a storm after Thanksgiving. This week, snap photos of places you like to ride and build a mental map of elevations and aspects that consistently hold snow. These are the areas where avalanche danger will rise quickly once the snow arrives.

Images.caption: Looking west from the top of Loveland Pass on November 15. You can see there isn't quite enough snow to overcome surface roughness on these north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, but maybe enough to form a weak layer in the future.
Images.altText: A rounded alpine ridge with patchy snow cover

Images.caption: The north-facing slopes of Red Peak from Hoosier Pass on November 12. This is one of the snowier areas in the Northern Mountains right now.
Drifts of firm snow like this are areas to be cautious. Imagine sliding into the sharp rocks below.
Images.altText: Sunlit evergreen branches in the lower left foreground overlook a shaded, wind-rippled snow slope descending toward a dark treeline, with a sunlit, pine-dotted mountainside rising across the valley.

Images.caption: Weak grains like this depth hoar found at Guanella Pass will be problematic once we get a large storm.
